speakers: Alan Dunne (co-host, macro and CTA analyst)
summary:
Weekly Systematic Investor episode: Dunne and Kaastrup-Larsen discuss Fed easing and neutral rate, Rogoff on inflation volatility, the yen carry unwind (BIS), trend-following August update and Asness's paper on high-volatility alternatives.
Theme: high-volatility uncorrelated components are capital-efficient with cheap futures leverage, and trend followers have zero (not negative) equity correlation.
Main conclusions: data-dependent Fed implies higher rate vol; carry regime fragile; institutions over-prefer low-vol products.

Rogoff inflation forecast; central bank independence and carry; labour bargaining shift
multi-manager vs carry regime; Fed easing cycle and 25 vs 50

trend following August update, fixed income dispersion

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: this year it was all about a transmission mechanism of monetary policy which is interesting that that's the thing that the policy makers are grappling with
claims.claim: Jackson Hole's theme each year shows what policymakers see as the dominant macro problem (2022 supply constraints, 2023 debt, 2024 transmission of rate hikes), a read on the policy regime.
claims.testable: no - qualitative reading of a speech theme

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Europe needs to invest uh 800 billion euros a year for the next number of years which is U about four and a half% of GDP
claims.claim: Draghi's report calls for about 800bn euros a year (4.5% of GDP, double the Marshall Plan) of European investment and common debt, a potentially far-reaching fiscal and industrial-policy shift if politics allow.
claims.indicator: EU investment plan size, common debt issuance
claims.direction: European growth/productivity up, common safe asset supply up
claims.conditions: only if European policymakers agree; the speaker doubts delivery
claims.testable: no - political outcome, no signal defined

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: he's saying yeah we're entering a period where volatility uh is going be higher
claims.claim: Rogoff expects periodic supply shifts that make inflation higher and more volatile, so the post-2022 regime has higher macro volatility than the prior decades.
claims.testable: no - regime view, hard to test

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: he just thinks we're going to find more situations where they take a chance on inflation Rising rather than having high unemployment
claims.claim: Central banks will increasingly accept higher inflation rather than higher unemployment when a supply shock hits, because political support for fighting inflation is thinner than for protecting jobs.
claims.indicator: central bank reaction to supply shocks
claims.conditions: when the choice is between inflation and unemployment

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: we'll have one more episode like the inflation surge that we've had we'll have another one like that in the next seven or eight years
claims.claim: Rogoff forecasts another inflation surge like 2021-22 within seven to eight years, so disinflation should not be extrapolated as a permanent solution.
claims.conditions: a supply-side shift that policymakers choose to accommodate

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I think the whole carry regime is reliant on trust in central banks
claims.claim: The decades-long carry regime depends on trust in central bank independence; losing it (e.g. political control of the Fed) could trigger bond vigilantes and break the regime.
claims.conditions: if a political winner takes control of the central bank

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: unions were strong the the employ you know workers were strong employers not so and then it shifted and for two or three decades for for sure employers were had the upper hand
claims.claim: Labour bargaining power has swung back from employers toward workers (shrinking labour force, behavioural change), which is a structural source of wage and inflation pressure.
claims.testable: partly - labour share and wage series exist, anecdotal here

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: large multi manager hedge funds that they had suffered their first outflow of Assets in seven years uh a decline of aom of 30 billion
claims.claim: Multi-manager hedge funds saw their first asset outflow in seven years (about $30bn) after performance disappointment, saturation of allocation, and pass-through fees, a sentiment shift for a crowded strategy.
claims.testable: partly - AUM flow data exist, one datapoint

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: a lot of big institutions looked at portfolios and said okay we're we're way overweight on the privates we to allocate the Hedge hes and getting the multi-manager kind of Diversified exposure was a quick and easy way
claims.claim: Multi-manager inflows were partly a one-off rebalancing out of overweight private markets into a one-stop diversified hedge fund allocation, so the flow driver may be exhausted.
claims.indicator: institutional allocation shifts from privates to hedge funds

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: pass through model where you know all of the expenses flow through to the uh investor and in aggregate that can account to you know up to 10% of
claims.claim: Pass-through expense models can take up to about 10% of the allocation, so multi-manager investors tend to balk once performance slows.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they seem to be gravitating towards perhaps the most expensive strategy of all with the least transparency
claims.claim: Institutions demand low fees and transparency from CTAs yet allocate heavily to expensive, opaque multi-managers and private equity, an inconsistency that reflects convenience over stated principles.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: a lot of these multistat strategies they're they're neutral they're Market neutral a lot of them and so in in a sense it goes back to our conversation with Kevin on the carry regime
claims.claim: Market-neutral multi-strategy funds harvest small inefficiencies with high leverage that works in a stable carry regime, so a change in market structure or volatility regime could hurt their returns as assets grow.
claims.direction: multi-strat returns down if carry regime ends
claims.conditions: fails when volatility rises and carry trades unwind; capacity limits on diversified return streams

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: signaling an easing cycle so I think that's an important point
claims.claim: Powell's Jackson Hole speech signalled the start of an easing cycle, not just a September cut, so the destination of policy matters more than the 25 versus 50bp debate.
claims.testable: partly - Fed path can be traded, but one event

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: actually what we've seen from the FED in the past you know in 2000 easing cycle 2007 there's a 25 and if things get bad then
claims.claim: Historically the Fed opens easing cycles with 25bp and moves to inter-meeting or larger cuts only when conditions deteriorate (2001, 2007), the typical playbook.
claims.testable: yes - historical Fed cycles can be tabulated

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: now for a long time that was 2 and a half% if you go back to 2019 if you go even 2021 22 even up to last year uh it was always 2 and a half%
claims.claim: The Fed's long-run neutral rate estimate (long-term dot) was 2.5% for years and has been edged up to about 2.8% in recent projections, with arguments for 3% on productivity and fiscal expansion.
claims.indicator: FOMC long-term fed funds rate projection (r-star)

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it could be anywhere from probably probably I would guess two and a half to three and a half you know but it still leaves a lot of easing
claims.claim: Neutral rate is unobservable in real time (range roughly 2.5-3.5%), so with policy at 5-5.25% there is still much easing room, which the market prices as about 100bp by year end.
claims.indicator: fed funds futures pricing vs neutral rate
claims.testable: partly - futures pricing observable, neutral not

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the market is I so my interpretation of what the market is saying is yeah we're moving towards um neutral but it's also pricing in a bit of recession risk as well
claims.claim: Market pricing of rates near 3% by mid-next year equals a move to neutral plus some probability of going below neutral on recession risk (one forecaster calls for 2%).
claims.testable: partly - comparison of curve vs neutral estimate

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you get a minus 100 payrolls they'll almost certainly have to cut 50 basis points at the next meeting because
claims.claim: A data-dependent Fed reacts quickly to weak data: a very negative payrolls print would force a 50bp cut at once, so rate moves become more reactive to individual releases.
claims.direction: front-end yields down on weak payrolls
claims.testable: yes - event study of rates vs payrolls surprises

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: as soon as you get any kind of significant weak data uh you'll immediately get a reaction and probably see that points to me being much more volatility in rates going ahead
claims.claim: The shift from forecast-based to data-dependent policy means higher rates volatility around data releases and around political risk such as the US election.
claims.conditions: while the Fed is explicitly data dependent
claims.testable: yes - rates vol vs regime of guidance

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there's a very high correlation then with that coming into to into play that being the new way of doing things and the extreme carry regime we saw exactly after that
claims.claim: Forward guidance, introduced after the financial crisis, coincides with the extreme carry regime; central banks are accused of facilitating it by suppressing volatility.
claims.direction: carry strategies up, volatility down under guidance

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: long end rates could be at three or six and the equity Market could be up or down and credit spreads could be tighter or not you know so the this idea that there's one rate
claims.claim: Policy stance cannot be summarised by one short rate: long yields, equities and credit spreads determine overall financial conditions, so policy can still be loose when the policy rate is called restrictive.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we saw this transition from having short exposure from a trend falling perspective to fixed income for more than two years and then slowly in the early summer and over the summer um exposure was caught
claims.claim: Trend followers were short bonds for over two years and flipped long during summer 2024, just in time to capture the August bond rally; fixed income drove sector returns.
claims.direction: long bonds after the trend turned
claims.testable: yes - CTA sector returns by period

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: we saw this at the back end of last year kind of in December in January the you know bonds rallied from kind of November and some managers were were faster to get on that
claims.claim: Speed of trend models creates dispersion: faster managers gain when a reversal persists and slower ones win when it reverses again, as seen in Dec-Jan and again in summer 2024.
claims.conditions: at turning points where a trend reverses repeatedly
claims.testable: yes - fast vs slow lookback comparison

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: fixed income is playing now from a risk perspective it has it was quite muted actually during uh many months and now we're back to it being maybe the largest exposure
claims.claim: Fixed income was a muted risk contributor for many months and has returned to being the largest exposure in trend portfolios, so risk allocation shifts with volatility and signal strength.
claims.testable: yes - risk allocation can be measured

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: sock gen CTA up 81 basis points in September up 2.15% for the year s Trend up about 1% up 2.34 for the year
claims.claim: CTA indices were modestly positive in 2024 (SG CTA +2.15% YTD, SG Trend +2.34%) while S&P 500 total return was +18.5%, so trend followers lagged equities.
claims.indicator: SG CTA Index, SG Trend Index, S&P 500 total return

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they have an estimate of the carry trade at $250 billion and they actually probably on the low side
claims.claim: BIS puts the yen carry trade near $250bn but components (hedge funds, interbank flows, yen loans, secured notes) mean it is larger; CFTC positioning shows only a small fraction of the position.
claims.indicator: yen carry trade size, CFTC yen positioning
claims.testable: partly - BIS estimate, but component data are incomplete

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: CT were heavily short Yen and they were just unwinding their short Yen all of that side
claims.claim: CTAs were short yen going into the unwind, so they contributed by covering shorts rather than by going long yen as the BIS paper implied.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: periods of low volatility encourage greater leverage and and that's that's kind of the nature of the system
claims.claim: Low volatility lowers margin requirements and raises leverage; when volatility spikes, exchange margin increases, margin calls and volatility-adjusted position cuts force deleveraging and degrossing.
claims.testable: yes - volatility regime and later drawdowns

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: October uh 1997 um you know the S&P was down 67% end of October one day uh big move you know but um you know twice as is the move we saw this time
claims.claim: The market and media reaction to moves is more intense now (real-time monitoring, social media): the Aug 2024 S&P drop was half the October 1997 drop yet drew calls for emergency Fed cuts, so perceived stress is larger than arithmetic moves.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: nobody wants downside volatility not even the central Banks
claims.claim: After 20 years of conditioning by the Fed put, investors and officials react to even modest drawdowns from all-time highs as emergencies.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: we can have v-shaped recoveries that are really painful for a trend follow or like maybe like covid where it took like a month
claims.claim: V-shaped recoveries hurt trend followers because they flip positions and are caught on both sides; position size changes from the volatility spike mattered more than the direction change.
claims.conditions: fast V-shaped reversals within a month
claims.testable: yes - trend returns around sharp reversals

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you look at TL TLT ETF it's about 10% since the start of July so it you know it's it was a capital markets event deleveraging and degross the type of event where bonds do well
claims.claim: In a deleveraging or degrossing event bonds rally (TLT about +10% since July), supporting the diversifier role, but inflation-driven episodes like 2022 can make bonds and trend followers fall together.
claims.testable: yes - bond returns by event type

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Zin yuz zag implies negative correlation but obviously it's not it's it's zero correlation
claims.claim: Trend following has roughly zero correlation to equities, not negative, so periods when both lose are normal and do not make it an unreliable diversifier.
claims.indicator: correlation of CTA index to equities
claims.conditions: zero correlation means joint losses occur at times

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Cliff asens makes the point yeah doesn't mean that markets are more accurately priced uh just because data comes more quickly
claims.claim: Asness argues faster information has not made markets more efficient: value spreads between expensive and cheap stocks stay wide (as in 1999-2000 and 2019) even after adjusting for tech, so the premise that efficiency kills trend and value is weak.
claims.indicator: value spread between expensive and cheap stocks

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: that that works as long as the crowd is independent
claims.claim: Wisdom-of-crowds efficiency requires independent participants, but common information and social media may make investors herd, reducing the independence that keeps prices accurate.
claims.testable: no - paper is qualitative, no data

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: you don't want you probably don't want excessive volatility for your overall portfolio because if you think about the that the mathematics you know if you lose 50% then the portfolio has to make 100%
claims.claim: Volatility drags compound returns at portfolio level, but a high-volatility component can be beneficial if it is uncorrelated with the rest of the portfolio.
claims.conditions: component uncorrelated to the rest of the portfolio

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you had an investment that had a 66% chance of being up 100% or a 33% chance of being down 100% obviously that's high positive expected return
claims.claim: An uncorrelated high-volatility bet can add value with periodic total losses if the portfolio is rebalanced to the other assets and the bet is repeated.
claims.conditions: uncorrelated with the rest of the portfolio, rebalancing

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it would tend to actually allocate to the alss and not the bonds now that's partially because he assumed alss were zero correlated to equities where his Bonds were three
claims.claim: With alternatives assumed uncorrelated to equities and bonds correlated at 0.3, a 10% volatility optimizer favours alternatives over bonds in a stock-bond-alts mix, but the result depends on those assumptions.
claims.conditions: depends on assumed correlations and expected returns

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: what you can do then is you allocate a smaller amount you would then allocate some to bonds as well
claims.claim: Using a 25% volatility alternative instead of a 10% one lets investors allocate a smaller weight and add bonds, giving a more diversified portfolio with a better Sharpe ratio and return per unit of risk.
claims.direction: higher return per unit of portfolio risk

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: you're basically getting leverage priced at the you know the US overnight rate as opposed to the spread that your bank is going to charge you
claims.claim: High-volatility futures funds give cheap, available leverage priced near the overnight rate rather than at a bank margin spread of 2-4%, so they are more capital efficient than borrowing to lever a 60/40 portfolio.
claims.indicator: futures leverage vs bank financing spread

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: institutions seem to prefer the lowall um I I don't I don't know why that is
claims.claim: Institutions prefer low-volatility (8-10%) alternative products while family offices and others accept 20% volatility, probably because boards and committees dislike explaining large drawdowns.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: sharp was invented for portfolios not for single uh strategies
claims.claim: Sharpe ratio is a portfolio-level metric and misleads when applied to single strategies; maximum drawdown relative to volatility should also be examined, where some volatile CTAs have much smaller drawdowns than their volatility suggests.
claims.indicator: Sharpe ratio, max drawdown to volatility

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: when they started aqr their first offering was a high Val strategy and immediately went into a draw down
claims.claim: High-volatility strategies face behavioural resistance and transition risk (the first 3-6 months after allocation), and 'give me half the amount' arguments do not persuade investors.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: volatility of 20 25% annualized were perfectly normal that was kind of what we did
claims.claim: CTA volatility of 20-25% was normal in 1990 when the industry was under $10bn; institutionalisation from 2000 and AUM growth to about $400bn pushed managers to lower leverage, which also let them manage more money.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the alpha is the alpha so if there's another 4% interest income it really just falls back to the investor
claims.claim: With zero rates institutions favoured low-volatility CTAs; as interest rates rise, the alpha is unchanged and interest income adds directly to investor returns, raising interest in higher-return versions.
claims.indicator: cash interest rates and CTA returns
claims.direction: CTA total return up with cash rates
claims.testable: yes - CTA excess return vs cash

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: regulation does prevent you from running uh full leverage in in in my world uh full leverage you you can't really get there
claims.claim: UCITS VaR limits cap leverage, so UCITS CTA products run around 15-16% volatility versus 20%+ in non-regulated versions.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: combining traditional assets with non-correlated return stream such as Trend following uh that that isn't a uh produces a safer and higher returning portfolio
claims.claim: Combining traditional assets with a non-correlated return stream like trend following gives a safer, higher-returning portfolio; the speaker says no white paper contradicts this.
